lesson_title: Semiotics: Signs, Codes and Connotation
content_html:
What Is a Sign?

Every time you look at a media product — a magazine cover, a music video thumbnail, a newspaper front page — you are reading a system of signs. The Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure argued that a sign is made up of two parts: the signifier (the form the sign takes — a word, an image, a colour, a sound) and the signified (the concept or idea it brings to mind). A red rose as a signifier calls up the idea of romance as its signified — but only because a culture has agreed that this connection means something.

Roland Barthes, the French cultural critic, extended this into media analysis. He argued that media products communicate on two levels. Denotation is the literal, surface-level meaning: a photograph of a young woman in a white dress denotes a young woman in a white dress. Connotation is the associated meaning layered on top: the white dress connotes purity, celebration, marriage — meanings that depend entirely on the cultural context in which the image is read.

Key Fact

A sign = signifier (the form) + signified (the concept). Denotation is the literal meaning; connotation is the cultural, associated meaning layered on top.

Types of Sign: Icon, Index and Symbol

Semioticians distinguish three types of sign, a classification useful for analysing how different media forms convey meaning. An iconic sign looks like what it represents — a photograph of a dog is iconic because it resembles a real dog. An index sign has a causal or physical connection to what it represents — smoke connotes fire, a sun-bleached headline connotes an old newspaper. A symbolic sign has a purely arbitrary, culturally agreed connection: there is nothing inherently “stoppy” about the colour red — its meaning at a traffic light is a social convention.

In practice, most media signs work at more than one level. A magazine cover photograph is iconic (it resembles the celebrity), but the celebrity’s pose, expression and styling also carry symbolic connotations about gender, aspiration or threat. Reading media products means unpicking all these levels simultaneously.

Signs do not float in isolation. They are organised into codes — systems of signs with rules that a particular community has learned. When a media producer places a man in a dark suit against a plain background on a professional LinkedIn-style profile image, they are deploying a dress code, a colour code and a composition code simultaneously. Readers who know those codes decode the image as “authority” or “business professional” without consciously analysing it.

Barthes identified five codes at work in narratives and texts: the enigma code (unresolved puzzles that pull audiences in), the action code (sequences that suggest what comes next), the semantic code (signs that carry connotations beyond their literal meaning), the symbolic code (deeper oppositions such as good vs. evil), and the referential code (references to wider cultural knowledge). For GCSE, the most important are the enigma code and the semantic code, as they appear directly in exam questions about how texts create suspense and carry connotations.

Anchorage and Polysemy

Images are naturally open to multiple interpretations. If you showed a close-up photograph of two clenched fists to different people, some might read conflict, others might read solidarity, others might read protest. Barthes called this quality polysemy. Because polysemy could leave a message uncontrolled, media producers often use text to pin down which meaning the audience should take from an image.

Barthes called this fixing function anchorage. A press photograph of a politician in a hard hat and high-visibility jacket is ambiguous — is the politician being praised for visiting a factory, or mocked for a photo opportunity? The headline anchors the meaning, directing the reader towards one interpretation. Advertisers use anchorage constantly: a perfume advertisement might show an ambiguous close-up of two bodies, and the brand name and slogan anchor the connotations towards desire and luxury rather than anything else.

Key Fact

Polysemy = an image can mean more than one thing. Anchorage = text (headline, caption, slogan) fixes the preferred meaning. Together they explain why media products combine image and text.

The Linear Model of Communication

Early communication theory modelled meaning as a simple, one-way process: a sender encodes a message and transmits it to a receiver who decodes it. A newspaper editor (sender) writes a front-page story (message) that readers (receivers) read. This linear model is useful as a starting point but it has clear limitations: it implies a passive audience who simply receive meaning, and it ignores the noise, mediation and context that shape how messages are actually understood.

The linear model is still useful in the exam as a framework for labelling who makes a media product and who consumes it, particularly in advertising and broadcasting contexts. However, the rise of social media and user-generated content has complicated the model: receivers are now also senders, and the direction of communication is often circular rather than linear.

Mode of address is the way a media product speaks to its audience — both literally in language choices and visually through the gaze of subjects in images. Direct address occurs when a figure in an image looks straight into the camera, creating a sense of personal connection: many magazine cover stars use direct address to pull buyers off the shelf. Indirect address places the audience as an observer rather than a participant, which is more common in photojournalism and in certain forms of lifestyle photography where the audience is invited to observe a scene rather than be spoken to directly.

Register refers to the level of formality in a text’s language and overall tone. A broadsheet newspaper uses a formal register to signal authority and reliability; a teen lifestyle magazine uses colloquial language and slang to create a sense of shared identity with its young readership. Register shapes connotations about the audience a product is aimed at and the relationship the producer wants to build with them.

Applying Semiotics: A Worked Example

Consider a typical tabloid newspaper front page covering a major sporting event. The denotation includes a large action photograph of a player, a bold headline in a large font, and a pullquote in a contrasting colour. The connotations are layered: the low-angle photograph connotes heroism and power; the choice of bright red for the headline connotes excitement and urgency (a symbolic code based on cultural convention); the pullquote in the athlete’s own words creates direct address even though the athlete is not looking at the camera. The anchorage — the headline text — pins down whether the story celebrates a victory or laments a defeat. A student who can unpick all these layers using precise terminology (denotation, connotation, anchorage, mode of address, code) is working at the highest level of media language analysis.

lesson_title: Selection, Combination and the Construction of Reality
content_html:
Media Products Are Always Constructed

One of the most important ideas in Media Studies is deceptively simple: media products do not show the world as it is — they construct a version of it. Every photograph, news broadcast, social media post and music video is the result of thousands of choices made by producers: which camera angle to use, which moment to capture, which words to include in a headline, which voices to interview. The audience sees only the result of those choices, not the choosing itself.

The process by which producers make and arrange those choices is called selection and combination. What is selected shapes meaning. What is left out — exclusion — shapes meaning just as powerfully, but is invisible to the audience who never sees what was cut.

Key Fact

Selection = what the producer chooses to include. Combination = how those elements are arranged together. Exclusion = what is deliberately left out. All three shape the meanings audiences take from media products.

The Rules of Media Language

Media producers do not select and combine elements at random — they follow the established conventions of the form they are working in. A broadsheet newspaper front page follows recognisable rules about column widths, headline hierarchies, image placement and caption style. A pop music video follows conventions about narrative structure, editing pace and the relationship between sound and image. These shared rules are what make a product recognisable as belonging to its form.

Audiences have internalised these rules so thoroughly that violations feel jarring. If a music video cuts on the beat it feels natural; if it cuts against the beat it creates deliberate tension or disorientation. If a news photograph is taken from eye level it implies equality; if taken from a low angle it implies power. These are the rules of media language that producers follow, subvert or exploit to construct particular meanings.

The process of making choices about which signs and codes to include in a product is called encoding. When a magazine editor chooses a close-up photograph of a celebrity rather than a mid-shot, selects a particular headline font, and positions the coverline text in a specific relationship to the image, they are encoding a set of meanings into that cover. Those choices are not neutral — they reflect the values, assumptions and commercial interests of the producer and the institution they work for.

The meaning that the producer intends the audience to take away is called the preferred meaning. However, audiences do not always take the preferred meaning — they bring their own experience, values and knowledge to the act of reading. A tabloid newspaper front page about immigration may encode a preferred meaning of alarm, but readers who personally identify with the communities being described may decode the same page very differently. This gap between encoding and decoding is explored more fully in the Media Representations and Media Audiences units.

Framing and Verisimilitude

Framing is the practice of presenting a subject matter from a particular viewpoint. It is not merely technical (the physical frame of a camera shot) but ideological: who is centred in the frame, who is marginalised, who is given a voice and who is absent all reflect choices that carry meaning. A documentary about urban poverty that interviews only economists and politicians frames poverty differently from one that centres the experiences of people living in it.

Despite all this construction, media products are often experienced as natural or real. Verisimilitude is the impression of truth — the convincing surface that makes a soap opera feel like real life, or a news broadcast feel like a transparent window on events. The more convincingly a product deploys the conventions of realism (handheld camera movement, naturalistic lighting, improvised-sounding dialogue), the more verisimilitude it achieves, and the harder it becomes for audiences to see the construction behind it.

Key Fact

Verisimilitude = the convincing impression of reality. Media products construct reality through choices of selection, combination, framing and exclusion — but are often consumed as if they are simply showing the world as it is.

Mediation and Points of View

Mediation describes what happens between an event and the audience’s understanding of it. Events do not reach audiences directly — they are processed through the interests, assumptions and technical conventions of media institutions. A football match is mediated by the choice of camera angles, commentary, slow-motion replays and edited highlights packages. A political speech is mediated by which thirty seconds the news chooses to air, what framing shot is used, and what the presenter says before and after the clip.

This means that all media products encode points of view — even products that claim to be neutral or objective. A documentary that presents a single line of argument encodes a clear viewpoint; a news report that selects only certain voices encodes assumptions about whose perspective counts as authoritative; a fashion photograph that presents one body type as desirable encodes a particular set of values about gender and aspiration. Part of Media Studies is developing the critical vocabulary to identify these encoded points of view rather than accepting them as natural.

Consider how a typical quality broadsheet newspaper and a typical tabloid newspaper might each cover the same news event — say, a large public demonstration. The broadsheet might select a wide establishing shot showing the scale of the crowd, combine it with a formal headline measuring the number of attendees, and include a quote from an academic expert. The tabloid might select a tight close-up of a single confrontational moment, combine it with an emotive headline foregrounding disruption, and quote a politician warning about public order.

Both newspapers have covered the same event. But through different acts of selection (which image, which voice), combination (how image and headline relate) and exclusion (what each leaves out), they have constructed two very different versions of reality. Neither is simply “the truth” — both are mediated constructions. Recognising this is at the heart of media literacy.

lesson_title: Narrative Theory: Propp, Todorov and Audience Engagement
content_html:
Why Narrative Theory Matters

Stories are among the oldest and most powerful tools in any media producer’s toolkit. Whether you are watching a streaming drama, reading a comic strip, playing a video game or watching a music video with a story thread, you are experiencing a narrative. Media Studies asks you to analyse how narratives are constructed, who they centre, and what that construction tells us about the values and assumptions of the producer. Two theorists are central to this analysis at GCSE level: Vladimir Propp and Tzvetan Todorov.

Vladimir Propp: Character Functions

The Russian folklorist Vladimir Propp analysed a large collection of folk tales in his 1928 work Morphology of the Folktale and found that, despite the variety of stories, the same types of character appeared repeatedly. Propp argued that these character types — which he called character functions — were structurally essential to the narrative: the story could not proceed without each role being filled, though one character could fill more than one role.

The seven character functions Propp identified are: the hero (who undertakes the quest), the villain (who creates the central conflict), the donor (who gives the hero a special gift, skill or object), the helper (who supports the hero), the princess or sought-for person (who is typically the goal or reward of the quest), the dispatcher (who sends the hero on the quest), and the false hero (who appears heroic but is not). At GCSE, you are expected to know and apply these seven types, not Propp’s full list of 31 narrative functions.

Key Fact

Propp’s seven character functions: hero, villain, donor, helper, princess (sought-for person), dispatcher, false hero. One character can fill more than one role. Source: Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (1928).

Propp developed his theory from folk tales, but the functions travel well into modern media. In a typical superhero film, the hero is clearly the protagonist with abilities; the villain creates the central threat; a mentor figure or organisation often acts as both dispatcher and donor (setting the hero on their mission and supplying them with tools or training); a sidekick fills the helper role; and a love interest or protected community represents the princess function. A false hero might be a colleague who seems trustworthy but proves to be compromised.

Propp is also useful for critiquing media products. When a narrative consistently places women only in the princess function (passive, to be rescued) or gives all the active hero and villain roles to men, Propp’s framework gives you precise language to describe this pattern. Conversely, when a media product subverts Propp by making the princess the hero, or by making the donor the villain, you can describe that subversion precisely and explain what meaning it creates. Exam questions sometimes ask you to apply Propp to a media product you have studied, so practise mapping character functions onto at least one television drama and one other narrative media form.

Tzvetan Todorov: Equilibrium and Disruption

The Bulgarian narratologist Tzvetan Todorov argued that most narratives follow a five-stage arc. They begin with an equilibrium — a state of normality or balance at the start of the story. A disruption then breaks that equilibrium, setting the narrative in motion. A period of recognition (the characters acknowledge that something has gone wrong) leads to an attempt to repair the disruption. Finally a new equilibrium is reached — which is not identical to the opening state, because the characters and their world have been changed by events.

This five-stage structure (equilibrium → disruption → recognition → repair → new equilibrium) is sometimes compressed in shorter media forms. A television advertisement for an insurance company might open with a couple contentedly driving (equilibrium), show their car being hit (disruption), and close with them smiling after a smooth insurance claim (new equilibrium). A music video narrative might move through the same arc in three minutes. The structure is useful precisely because it is flexible enough to apply across all narrative media forms.

Key Fact

Todorov’s narrative arc: (1) equilibrium → (2) disruption → (3) recognition → (4) repair → (5) new equilibrium. The new equilibrium is never identical to the opening one — the narrative has changed things.

Enigma and Closure

Both Propp and Todorov help explain the structure of narratives, but neither fully explains why audiences keep watching or reading. Two concepts borrowed from Roland Barthes’s code theory are particularly useful here. The enigma code describes the unresolved questions that a narrative plants early and answers only gradually — the classic “who did it?” of a crime drama, or the ambiguous opening image of a thriller. Audiences engage with narratives partly to resolve enigmas.

Closure is the satisfying resolution of those enigmas — the detective names the murderer, the hero defeats the villain, the couple reunite. Closed narratives (those that resolve all their threads) are associated with mainstream entertainment. Open narratives (those that deliberately leave questions unanswered) are associated with art-house or prestige media. A streaming drama might use a cliff-hanger ending to deny closure deliberately and compel audiences to watch the next episode — a commercial use of the enigma code to drive continued engagement.

Todorov’s arc assumes a linear narrative — one that moves chronologically from beginning to end. Many mainstream media products do follow this structure because it is the most immediately accessible for audiences. However, non-linear narratives deliberately disrupt chronological order, using flashbacks, flash-forwards or multiple perspectives to create different effects: mystery (we see the aftermath before the cause), empathy (a flashback gives us a character’s backstory before a key decision), or complexity (simultaneous storylines that converge).

Non-linear narratives are common in prestige television, literary fiction adaptations and video games, where the audience’s active role in exploring the narrative is part of the experience. For Media Studies analysis, identifying whether a narrative is linear or non-linear is the first step — the more interesting question is always: what effect does that structural choice have on how audiences engage with the product?

lesson_title: Technology and the Form of Media Products
content_html:
Technology Shapes What Media Products Are

Media products are not created in a vacuum — every product is shaped by the technologies available to make it, distribute it and consume it. A newspaper from the 1890s looks nothing like a digital news feed, not just because the content has changed, but because the technologies of production, distribution and consumption are completely different. When new technologies arrive, they change what it is possible to create, who can create it and how audiences experience it.

Production technology determines what images and sounds a producer can capture and craft. Distribution technology determines how finished products reach audiences — whether by broadcast signal, physical disc, streaming server or social media algorithm. Consumption technology determines the conditions under which audiences experience the product — a shared public cinema is a very different context from a private smartphone screen. All three dimensions matter for media analysis.

Key Fact

Three dimensions of technology: production (how it is made), distribution (how it reaches audiences) and consumption (how audiences experience it). New technologies transform all three simultaneously.

Computer-Generated Imagery (CGI)

Computer-generated imagery (CGI) has fundamentally transformed what is possible in screen media. Before digital production, visual effects relied on miniature models, matte paintings, puppetry and practical in-camera techniques. CGI made it possible to create photorealistic environments, creatures, crowds and physical effects that would be impossible, prohibitively expensive or dangerous to achieve practically. The scale and texture of environments visible in contemporary action films, fantasy series and video games are products of this technology.

CGI does more than add spectacle — it changes the connotations and verisimilitude of media products. A historical drama can digitally recreate a city as it appeared centuries ago. A superhero film can place a character against a photorealistic alien landscape. These capabilities alter audience expectations: consumers of high-budget screen media now expect a level of visual credibility that was technically impossible a generation ago, and the absence of it reads as low-budget or amateurish. CGI has also made it possible to alter the appearance of real people — ageing actors digitally, smoothing skin, changing body proportions — which raises significant questions about representation and authenticity.

High definition (HD) and its successors (4K, 8K) changed the sensory quality of moving-image media. Where standard-definition television had a grainy, slightly distanced quality, HD delivers images of extreme clarity that can make a drama feel more documentary-like in its immediacy. This hyper-realism has aesthetic consequences: make-up, prosthetics and physical sets that were convincing in standard definition can appear artificial in HD close-ups, requiring significant investment to maintain believability.

HD also changed shooting styles. The increased sensitivity of HD cameras means producers can use lower light levels, which has enabled a more naturalistic, less artificially lit aesthetic in prestige drama. Conversely, the extreme clarity of HD has encouraged some music video and advertising directors to use stylised, deliberately lo-fi aesthetics — grainy film stock looks, VHS textures — as a countercultural signal against the corporate smoothness of high-definition commercial media.

Image Manipulation and Authenticity

Image manipulation has made the photograph an increasingly unreliable document of reality. In advertising, beauty, fashion and celebrity media, digital retouching is standard practice: skin is smoothed, bodies are reshaped, backgrounds are replaced, blemishes removed. The result is an image that presents an idealised version of a person or product that may never have existed in front of the camera.

This matters for Media Studies because it is central to questions of representation: the body types, skin tones and facial features presented as “normal” or “aspirational” in manipulated images are constructions. Audiences who internalise these as realistic standards are responding to a constructed reality rather than the diversity of human appearance. Debates about the regulation of image manipulation in advertising — particularly in relation to body image and the audiences these products target — are ongoing. Some media organisations have introduced labelling requirements for digitally altered images; others resist this as an interference with creative freedom.

Key Fact

Image manipulation allows producers to alter photographs digitally, shaping what audiences perceive as ‘normal’ or ‘aspirational’ appearance. It is central to debates about representation, authenticity and the responsibility of media producers.

Mobile Communication Technology and User-Generated Content

Mobile communication technology has transformed both who can create media and where media can be consumed. A smartphone in a pocket is simultaneously a high-definition camera, a video editor, a broadcasting studio and a media consumption device. The barrier to media production has fallen dramatically: the equipment required to make a video that could reach millions of viewers is now available to almost anyone with a mid-range phone and a social media account.

The content produced by ordinary people rather than professional media organisations is called user-generated content (UGC). UGC has complicated the linear model of communication: audiences are now also producers. A spectator at a news event can film it and publish it before the professional news crews arrive. A consumer of a music video can create a response or parody and distribute it globally. This blurring of the producer/consumer distinction — sometimes captured in the term “prosumer” — has created new forms of media language and new questions about the quality, authenticity and reliability of media content.

Digital convergence describes the merging of previously distinct media technologies into single platforms and devices. A smart TV is simultaneously a broadcast receiver, a streaming client, a games console and a social media portal. This convergence has changed patterns of media consumption fundamentally: audiences no longer need to choose between television, radio, print and online media — they access all of these through the same device at the same time.

Streaming platforms have particularly transformed the relationship between production technology and audience behaviour. When audiences can access an entire series immediately rather than waiting for weekly broadcasts, producers can structure narratives differently, creating long-form story arcs that require consistent viewing across many hours. This “streaming-era” narrative form — with its complex characters, slow-burn development and cliff-hanger episode endings — is a direct product of the consumption technology available to contemporary audiences.

lesson_title: Codes, Conventions, Genre and Intertextuality
content_html:
Varieties of Code

In the previous lessons on semiotics, we met the general concept of a code — a shared system of signs with agreed rules. The specification asks you to understand three main varieties of code, each of which operates differently in different media forms: technical codes, symbolic codes, and verbal and non-verbal codes. Together, these form the vocabulary through which media products communicate.

Technical codes include all the choices made through equipment and editing: shot types (close-up, mid-shot, wide shot), camera movement (pan, tilt, tracking shot), editing pace, lighting style, and sound (diegetic, non-diegetic, dialogue). A low-angle shot makes a subject appear powerful. Fast cutting creates excitement. Diegetic sound (sound that comes from within the world of the product) creates realism; non-diegetic sound (added in post-production) creates mood or provides narrative information that characters cannot hear.

Symbolic codes are conveyed through the elements of mise-en-scène — the arrangement of everything visible in the frame. Costume codes signify character identity, social status and period. Colour codes carry connotations (red = danger or passion, white = purity or clinical neutrality, black = authority or threat, depending on context). Props, set dressing, location and the body language of performers all contribute symbolic meaning that an audience decodes without necessarily conscious analysis.

Key Fact

Technical codes = camera, editing, sound choices. Symbolic codes = mise-en-scène: costume, colour, props, location, body language. Both are used by producers to encode meaning into media products.

Verbal and Non-Verbal Codes

Verbal codes include all the choices made through language: the vocabulary of a headline, the formality of a presenter’s voice, the dialogue of characters in a drama. A tabloid newspaper’s punchy, colloquial headline deploys a different verbal code from a broadsheet’s formal, measured prose — both choices carry connotations about the assumed audience, the newspaper’s values and its relationship with readers.

Non-verbal codes are communicated without words: the posture of a model, the eye contact (or lack of it) between characters in a scene, the distance between figures in a photograph. These codes are particularly important in print and screen media where the audience cannot hear a voice — a slight downward tilt of the chin on a magazine cover, or crossed arms in a news photograph, can entirely change the connotations of a portrait.

Print and online media deploy a further set of codes specific to their form: house style is the set of consistent typographic, colour and layout conventions that make a publication instantly recognisable. The typeface of a broadsheet masthead connotes tradition and authority; the bold sans-serif of a tabloid connotes urgency and directness. Colour palettes carry institutional identity — audiences associate specific colours with specific publications, making those colours part of the publication’s brand code.

Typography is itself a code: the size, weight, placement and style of text on a page or screen encodes hierarchy (which information is most important), mood (a serif font feels different from a sans-serif font) and institutional character. The choice of juxtaposition — placing two images or text elements next to each other — creates meaning through their combination that neither element has alone. A celebrity portrait placed beside a headline about mental health creates a different meaning from the same portrait placed beside a headline about box-office success.

Genre: Repetition and Difference

The theorist Steve Neale argued that genre operates through the tension between repetition and difference. Audiences come to a horror film, a crime drama or a pop music video with a set of expectations — expectations about atmosphere, character types, narrative structure and visual style. The genre exists because those expectations have been confirmed by enough products to become conventions. But if every horror film were identical, audiences would lose interest: genre products must offer enough repetition to feel familiar and satisfying, but enough difference to feel fresh and surprising.

Neale also highlighted the genre cycle: genres are not stable — they evolve. A genre begins with early products establishing its conventions, develops through a period of refinement and intensification, moves towards self-parody (where products knowingly mock the genre’s own conventions), and either declines or transforms into something new. Understanding where a product sits in the genre cycle helps explain its codes and conventions: a product made early in a genre’s cycle will deploy conventions earnestly, while one made during the parody phase will deploy them ironically.

Key Fact

Steve Neale argued that genre operates through repetition (familiar conventions that satisfy audience expectations) and difference (fresh elements that prevent boredom). Genres evolve through a cycle of establishment, intensification, parody and transformation.

Hybridity and Intertextuality

Genre hybridity occurs when a media product combines the conventions of two or more genres. A romantic comedy draws on the character types and narrative arc of romance while also deploying the comic misunderstanding and verbal wit of comedy. A crime thriller mixes the procedural conventions of crime with the tension and urgency of the thriller. Hybrid genres are commercially appealing because they can target audiences from two genre communities simultaneously. Identifying which genre conventions have been combined, and in what proportions, is a key analytical task.

Intertextuality describes the practice of a media product referencing another. This can be explicit (a direct quote or parody of another product), implicit (a shared stylistic influence that audiences with relevant cultural knowledge will recognise), or structural (a narrative that consciously echoes the structure of a well-known earlier product). Intertextual references create a layered experience: audiences who recognise the reference get an additional pleasure — the in-joke, the nod to a shared cultural touchstone — while audiences who do not recognise it still engage with the product at the surface level. Music videos, advertising and social media content are especially rich in intertextual references because their short form rewards the compressed meaning that a well-chosen allusion can carry.

Consider a typical crime drama opening sequence. The technical codes include a palette of cool, desaturated colours (connoting bleakness and moral ambiguity), low-key lighting (connoting danger), and slow editing with careful use of close-ups on crime scene details (building enigma). The symbolic codes include a detective figure whose rumpled clothing connotes world-weariness, a crime scene location that connotes urban decay, and props (evidence bags, police tape) that signal the genre. Verbal codes include clipped, procedural dialogue that connotes professional detachment. Taken together, these codes construct a recognisable genre world: even before you know the plot, you know you are watching crime drama because the codes are so firmly established in this genre.

If this drama then deploys an intertextual reference — say, a character making an explicit comparison to a famous real-world case, or a visual quotation from a celebrated earlier crime series — audiences who recognise it get a richer experience. And if the drama subverts genre expectations — by making the detective the least reliable character, or by deploying warmth and colour rather than cold and shadow — it is exploiting audience familiarity with the genre’s conventions to create a surprise or a commentary on the genre itself.

lesson_title: Re-Presentation: Selection, Construction and Mediation
content_html:
What Does “Re-Presentation” Really Mean?

When you open a newspaper or watch the evening news, you might feel you are looking through a window at the world as it actually is. But media products do not simply capture reality — they re-present it. The hyphen matters: every image, headline and broadcast is the result of choices made by producers, editors and platforms before it ever reaches you.

This is one of the most important ideas in the whole of media studies. Once you understand that every media product is a constructed version of reality, you start asking different questions: who made these choices? What did they leave out? Whose point of view does this reflect?

Key Fact

Every media product is the result of three interlinked processes: selection (choosing what to include), construction (shaping the material into a product) and mediation (filtering the world through the values and perspectives of the producer).

Selection: What Gets In and What Gets Left Out

Selection operates at every stage of production. A photograph of a protest might show a peaceful crowd or a burning barricade — both may have happened, but only one image can appear on the front page. A news editor chooses which stories run, in what order, and how much space each receives. An advertiser chooses which product features to highlight and which to ignore. Every act of selection involves an act of exclusion: what is not shown matters just as much as what is.

Think about a typical front page of a quality daily newspaper. The editors receive hundreds of potential stories each day. Perhaps four or five make the front page. The rest are not shown to readers at all. The selection of those four or five stories, and the prominence given to each, already communicates a set of values about what is important in the world.

Construction: Turning Raw Material into a Product

Construction refers to how the raw material is assembled. A television news report about a local flooding event might begin with aerial drone footage showing submerged streets, cut to a close-up of a tearful resident, then include a statement from a local councillor, and end with a graphic showing predicted rainfall. None of those elements were inevitable — the reporter and editor constructed that sequence to tell a particular kind of story. Choices about framing, camera angle, music, editing pace and the order of speakers all shape the meaning audiences take away.

Mediation is the broadest of the three processes. Even when a producer tries to be objective, their choices are shaped by personal background, cultural context, employer expectations and commercial pressures. The journalist who grew up in a particular community, the broadcaster funded by advertisers, the social media algorithm designed to maximise engagement — all of these forces mediate what audiences see.

Mediation explains why two outlets can cover the same event in ways that feel almost unrecognisable to each other. The event itself has not changed; the filter through which it has passed is different. This is why developing media literacy — the habit of asking how a product was made and why — is so valuable.

Two Competing Views of Media and Reality

When scholars and media professionals debate how truthfully the media represent the world, two broad positions emerge. The first, sometimes called the “window on the world” view, holds that media products — especially factual ones like news — can and should aim for an accurate, transparent picture of events. On this view, bias and distortion are departures from a norm of objectivity that is possible in principle.

The second view, associated with the phrase “the medium is the message” (popularised by the media theorist Marshall McLuhan), argues that the form of a medium shapes meaning at least as much as its content. A photograph, a radio broadcast and a social media post covering the same event will produce fundamentally different meanings because each medium has its own logic, its own codes, its own relationship to time and audience. There is no neutral, transparent window — only different kinds of glass.

Key Fact

Marshall McLuhan argued that the properties of a medium — not just its content — shape the meaning audiences receive. A photograph communicates differently from radio or text even when covering the same story, because each medium involves different codes, different timing and a different relationship with its audience.

Re-presentation is not a neutral act — it positions the audience to read the product in a particular way. Audience positioning works through all the codes discussed in Media Language: camera angle, word choice, music, layout and the sequence in which information appears. A low-angle shot of a politician makes them seem powerful; a high-angle shot of the same person makes them seem small and vulnerable. Neither angle is ‘neutral’ — both are choices.

Producers typically try to build a preferred or dominant reading into their product — the interpretation they want audiences to take away. This preferred reading is never guaranteed, because audiences can and do resist or challenge it, but it is built into the structure of the product through selection, construction and mediation. Understanding this is what allows a media-literate viewer to read against the grain of a product and notice the ideology it carries.

Verisimilitude and the Appearance of Reality

Even clearly fictional products — a soap opera, a crime drama, an advertising lifestyle shoot — depend on appearing believable. Verisimilitude is the technical term for this appearance of reality. Producers use realistic settings, naturalistic dialogue, location filming and real-world problems to make audiences feel the product reflects something true about life. The more verisimilitude a product achieves, the more powerfully it can position audiences and communicate an ideology, because audiences are less likely to question what feels real.

lesson_title: Gender, Stereotypes and the Mulvey Male Gaze
content_html:
How Does Gender Get Represented?

Spend a few minutes flicking through a range of mainstream magazines, film posters or music videos and a pattern becomes visible: women and men are often depicted in distinctly different ways. Gender representation is concerned with how the media construct and communicate ideas about masculinity and femininity. These representations are never neutral — they reflect and reinforce assumptions about how men and women should look, behave and be valued.

Essentialism and Social Constructionism

There are two main theoretical positions on where gender comes from. Essentialism holds that the differences between men and women are biological and universal — rooted in nature rather than culture. On an essentialist account, media representations of women as nurturing or men as dominant are simply reflecting a natural reality.

The competing view is social constructionism. Social constructionists argue that gender is not fixed in biology but is produced and reproduced by cultural institutions — including the media. On this view, when a fashion magazine consistently shows women as passive and decorative, it is not reflecting nature but actively creating a norm about femininity. This norm then shapes how real people see themselves and each other.

Key Fact

Essentialism argues that gender differences are natural and biological; social constructionism argues they are produced by culture and society. Most contemporary media scholarship adopts a social constructionist position, because it can explain why gender representations change over time and vary across cultures.

Stereotypes: How They Work and Why They Matter

A stereotype is an oversimplified but widely recognised representation. Stereotypes are cognitive shortcuts: they allow audiences to process characters and situations instantly because the media has already established what certain types of people are ‘like’. A gruff older male detective. A vain teenage girl obsessed with looks. A nerdy male computer scientist. Each of these types draws on accumulated media representations to communicate a role rapidly.

Stereotypes do not only limit the groups they depict — they also reflect and reinforce the power relationships within society. Negative stereotypes tend to be applied to groups with less social power, reducing complex individuals to a single degrading trait. Positive stereotypes — the idea that a certain group is naturally gifted at music, or sport, or mathematics — can seem flattering but still remove individuality and place people in boxes they did not choose.

Stereotypes become established through repetition. When the same representation of a social group appears across hundreds of media products — across different genres, platforms and time periods — audiences begin to naturalise it. The stereotype starts to seem like an observation about reality rather than a constructed shorthand. This is why the same groups of people tend to be stereotyped in similar ways across otherwise very different media forms.

However, stereotypes are not fixed. They shift as social attitudes change. Compare the representation of working women in mainstream television from the 1960s with the 2020s and you will see significantly different norms. A counter-type actively subverts a familiar stereotype — a male nurse, a female action hero, an older woman shown as professionally authoritative — and signals to audiences that the norms are changing.

Laura Mulvey and the Male Gaze

The most influential feminist contribution to media studies on gender representation comes from film scholar Laura Mulvey. In her 1975 essay Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema, Mulvey argued that mainstream cinema structures visual pleasure around a male point of view. The camera habitually frames women as spectacles — to be looked at — while men are framed as active agents who drive the narrative.

Mulvey described three interlocking gazes that together create what she called the male gaze:

  • The camera’s gaze: the way the camera itself lingers on a female character’s body, fragments it into close-ups, or moves slowly across it.
  • The characters’ gaze: male characters within the narrative who look at female characters, positioning the audience to share their viewpoint.
  • The audience’s gaze: Mulvey argued that the film text invites all viewers — regardless of their own gender — to adopt a masculine, voyeuristic position when watching.
Key Fact

Mulvey identified three gazes: the camera’s gaze (how the camera films women), the characters’ gaze (male characters looking at women in the narrative) and the audience’s gaze (the viewer adopting a masculine viewpoint). Together they position women as objects of visual pleasure rather than active subjects.

Although Mulvey wrote specifically about cinema, media scholars have applied her argument across a wide range of forms. In a typical mainstream pop music video aimed at a mixed audience, a female performer might be filmed with slow camera movements, soft lighting and repeated close-ups of her face and body, while a male performer in the same video is shot from neutral angles that emphasise action. The camera choices encode gendered ways of looking even when the genre has nothing to do with narrative film.

Mulvey’s theory has also been critiqued and developed. The theorist bell hooks, writing about the experience of Black women viewers, argued for what she called an “oppositional gaze” — a refusal to identify with the positions offered by the mainstream text. This adds an important dimension to Mulvey’s model: the gaze is not only gendered but also racialised, and real audiences do not simply accept the viewing positions they are offered.

lesson_title: Producer Choices, Persuasion and Misrepresentation
content_html:
Why Do Producers Make the Choices They Do?

Every media product is the result of thousands of decisions: which angle to film from, which quote to use, whose face appears on the cover. These decisions do not happen randomly — they are shaped by the producer choices that reflect the purposes, values, commercial interests and ideological positions of the organisations and individuals behind the product.

Understanding producer choices means recognising that representations are not inevitable. There is always a human decision behind every image, headline and broadcast. And those decisions tend to cluster: producers working within the same institution, genre or commercial context make similar decisions that produce similar representations — which is how systematic patterns emerge across the media landscape.

Audience Positioning Through Producer Choices

Audience positioning is the practical outcome of producer choices. A news editor who places a story about immigration above a story about economic growth is already positioning readers to see one issue as more significant than the other. A documentary that interviews only one side of a debate and films the opposing side with unflattering close-ups is guiding the audience towards a clear preferred reading without stating that position openly.

Producers use a range of tools to position audiences. In print media, choice of photograph, headline wording, font size and page position all contribute. In broadcast, framing, editing rhythm, music and the order of contributors work together. In advertising, lighting, casting, voiceover tone and music choice are all selected to create a specific emotional and ideological response.

Key Fact

Producer choices shape audience positioning through the codes available in each medium: in print, these include headline language, image selection and page placement; in broadcast, framing, editing and music; in advertising, casting, lighting and voiceover. All of these choices can advance a selective or biased representation without appearing to do so openly.

Techniques of Persuasive Communication

Some media products aim explicitly to persuade — advertising, political campaigns and public information broadcasts all have persuasion as a primary purpose. Persuasive communication uses specific techniques to move audiences towards a desired attitude or behaviour.

Common techniques include: appealing to emotion (a charity advertisement showing a child in distress bypasses rational argument and directly triggers sympathy); appealing to authority (using experts, celebrities or statistics to make a claim seem credible); creating a sense of aspiration or fear (advertising often positions products as routes to a desirable life, or as protection against an undesirable one); and propaganda, in which a specific political viewpoint is presented as objective truth.

Political bias in media representation refers to the systematic tendency of an outlet to present events from a particular political perspective. This can be explicit — a newspaper with an openly stated editorial line — or more subtle, operating through spin: the careful framing of information to make it seem favourable to a particular party or policy without obviously misrepresenting facts.

A key tool of political representation is agenda-setting: the power to decide which issues receive attention and how much coverage they get. An outlet that consistently reports immigration as a problem but rarely reports its economic contributions is not necessarily lying — it is selecting and framing the story in a way that steers the audience towards a particular conclusion. This is a form of selective representation, and it operates differently from outright propaganda because it is harder for audiences to identify and challenge.

Misrepresentation, Under-Representation and Their Consequences

Misrepresentation occurs when a social group is depicted in ways that are inaccurate, one-sided or demeaning. Misrepresentation is not always deliberate: it can emerge from the cumulative effect of many producers making similar choices because they share similar backgrounds, work within similar institutions, or are under similar commercial pressures.

Under-representation is a related but distinct problem. When a social group — defined by ethnicity, disability, age, class or sexuality — is almost entirely absent from the media that most audiences consume, it sends a message about whose stories, lives and perspectives are considered worth showing. The sociologist George Gerbner, developing what he called cultivation theory, argued that heavy media consumers tend to absorb media representations as if they were a description of real social reality. If certain groups are absent from that representation, heavy viewers are likely to underestimate their presence and importance in society.

Key Fact

George Gerbner’s cultivation theory argues that long-term, heavy media consumption shapes viewers’ understanding of social reality. Groups that are under-represented or consistently misrepresented in mainstream media risk being seen as less important, less normal or more threatening than they actually are in society.

Tokenism occurs when producers include a single representative of a marginalised group — one Black character in an otherwise all-white cast, one disabled presenter on an otherwise abled panel — to create the impression of inclusion while leaving the overall pattern of representation unchanged. Tokenism does not address under-representation; it masks it.

A more extreme form is symbolic annihilation — the near-total absence or consistent trivialisation of a group in media representations. When a group is symbolically annihilated, their absence from the media communicates that their experiences, lives and perspectives do not count. Recognising these patterns is an important part of critically reading any media landscape.

lesson_title: Viewpoints, Self-Representation and the Social Significance of Representation
content_html:
Dominant and Contested Representations

Not all representations are equal. Some become so familiar and so widely repeated across media that they begin to feel like simple descriptions of reality rather than constructed choices. These are dominant representations. A dominant representation does not need to be accurate to be powerful — it simply needs to be everywhere. When audiences encounter the same representation of a social group across news programmes, drama series, advertising campaigns and social media simultaneously, that representation becomes difficult to challenge because it seems to come from all directions at once.

A contested representation is one that actively challenges the dominant version. Contested representations can emerge from alternative or independent media, from social media campaigns, from documentary film-making, or from community-led journalism. They often come from members of the social group that has been misrepresented, who bring a different perspective and set of experiences to the production process.

Viewpoints, Values and Messages in Representation

Every representation communicates a viewpoint. This viewpoint may be explicit — a documentary that openly argues for a political position — or implicit, embedded in the choices of framing, language and selection that structure the product. Even apparently neutral factual products carry viewpoints: the decision to describe a protestor as an ‘activist’ versus a ‘campaigner’ versus a ‘troublemaker’ encodes a value judgement in a single word choice.

Representations become especially significant when the same viewpoint is reinforced across multiple media products and platforms, creating what scholars call a dominant ideology. Audiences are more likely to absorb and internalise an ideological position when it appears to come from everywhere independently rather than from a single source.

Key Fact

Dominant representations are repeated widely across media products and come to seem natural. Contested representations challenge dominant versions and often emerge from communities or producers with direct experience of the group being represented. Both carry viewpoints that reflect particular values and ideological positions.

The Rise of Self-Representation

For most of media history, representations of social groups were produced almost entirely by professionals working within large institutions. Ordinary people had no effective way to represent themselves to a mass audience. Digital technologies and social media platforms have changed this fundamentally. Today, individuals can produce, publish and distribute media content to potentially global audiences with minimal equipment and no institutional backing.

The term prosumer describes someone who is both producer and consumer of media. The rise of the prosumer has created new possibilities for self-representation: individuals and communities can now tell their own stories, challenge dominant representations of their social group, and reach audiences that would previously have been inaccessible.

Social media influencers represent a new kind of media producer. An influencer who belongs to a marginalised group and builds an audience around their own life and perspective is, in a real sense, producing a self-representation that would never have existed in legacy media. User-generated content (UGC) on platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram has enabled entirely new kinds of representation to enter the mainstream.

However, these possibilities have limits. Social media platforms are commercial organisations governed by algorithms that prioritise certain kinds of content and suppress others. Self-representations that are radical, uncomfortable or counter to mainstream tastes may find their reach restricted. The prosumer revolution does not dissolve institutional power — it creates new institutions with new gatekeeping mechanisms. The question of whose self-representation gets amplified, and whose gets buried, is as important as the question of who gets to speak at all.

The Social, Cultural and Political Significance of Representation

Representation matters far beyond the screen. When a social group is consistently represented in limiting, demeaning or absent ways, it affects how that group is treated in the real world. Research across sociology and psychology has shown that people’s attitudes towards groups they have little direct experience with are heavily shaped by media exposure. A group that is always shown as threatening in news media tends to be feared more in daily life; a group that is always invisible tends to be seen as marginal.

The social significance of representation is also about aspiration and identity. When young people see people who look like them, share their background or face similar challenges represented positively and centrally in mainstream media, it signals that their experiences are worth telling and their potential is recognised. Conversely, absence or exclusively negative representation sends the opposite message. This is why debates about diversity in casting, editorial leadership and production teams are not just about aesthetics — they have direct social consequences.

Key Fact

Representation has real social consequences: how groups are shown in media shapes audience attitudes towards those groups in daily life. Positive, complex representation enables aspiration and recognition; negative or absent representation can reinforce social inequalities and shape how groups are treated.

One of the most politically significant forms of representation is news. News organisations do not simply report what happens — they set the agenda by deciding which events are worthy of coverage and which are not. Scholars Johan Galtung and Mari Ruge identified a set of factors — news values — that make events more likely to be selected for news coverage: these include proximity (how close to the audience), magnitude (how big or dramatic), negativity (bad news travels faster than good), continuity (ongoing stories hold audience attention) and elite persons or nations (stories about powerful people or countries).

The political significance of news values lies in what they systematically exclude: small-scale positive stories, long-term structural problems without dramatic moments, and the experiences of groups that do not have elite status. This means the news as a whole represents a particular kind of world — one that privileges drama, crisis and power — which shapes how audiences understand politics, society and which groups matter.

lesson_title: Audience Interpretation and Hall's Reception Theory
content_html:
How Do Audiences Read Media Representations?

Earlier lessons established that producers build preferred readings into their media products through selection, construction and mediation. But a preferred reading is never guaranteed. Different audiences — coming from different backgrounds, with different experiences and different relationships to the groups being represented — can and do read the same product in very different ways. The question of how audiences decode media representations is one of the most important in the whole subject.

The theoretical framework that best captures this is provided by the cultural theorist Stuart Hall’s encoding-decoding model. Hall’s model moved media studies away from the idea that audiences simply receive messages and towards the recognition that audiences actively interpret and sometimes resist what they are given.

Encoding and Decoding

Encoding is what happens at the production stage. Producers embed their preferred reading — the interpretation they want audiences to accept — into the text through all the techniques of media language: word choice, camera angle, music, editing, framing, image selection. The text is not neutral: it carries the ideological position of its producers, shaped by institutional pressures, commercial considerations and the dominant ideology of the society in which it was produced.

Decoding is what happens at the reception stage. Audiences bring their own experiences, social positions, cultural backgrounds and prior knowledge to a text when they interpret it. Hall argued that because of this, the meaning a producer intends to communicate and the meaning an audience actually takes away are not always the same.

Key Fact

Stuart Hall’s encoding-decoding model (1973) argues that media texts are encoded with a preferred meaning by producers, but audiences decode those texts in potentially different ways depending on their social position, experience and values. This means that the meaning of a media text is not fixed in the text itself — it is produced in the encounter between text and audience.

The Three Reading Positions

Hall identified three positions from which audiences can decode a media text:

The dominant or preferred reading is when an audience member accepts the preferred meaning the producer has encoded. They take the text at face value and interpret it broadly as the producer intended. A viewer who watches a news bulletin covering a public sector strike and comes away thinking “this will cause inconvenience for ordinary people” is largely accepting the preferred framing if that is what the bulletin emphasised.

The negotiated reading is the most common position in practice. The audience member accepts some elements of the preferred meaning but challenges or requalifies others. They might broadly accept the framing of a news story but resist one specific claim, or accept the narrative of a drama but identify the representation of a social group as stereotyped. The negotiated reader is neither fully compliant nor fully resistant.

The oppositional reading is when an audience member understands the preferred meaning but rejects it entirely. They decode the text from a different ideological standpoint. A trade union member watching the same news bulletin about a strike might read it as a corporate-friendly misrepresentation of workers’ legitimate demands — an entirely different interpretation of the same content.

Key Fact

Hall’s three reading positions are: dominant/preferred (audience accepts the producer’s preferred meaning), negotiated (audience partly accepts and partly challenges the preferred meaning) and oppositional (audience rejects the preferred meaning from a different ideological position). The negotiated reading is where most real audience reception sits.

Hall’s model explains why the same text can produce such different responses in different audiences, by pointing to the role of social variables. A member of the ethnic group being represented in a media product will typically bring very different knowledge and experience to that product than someone from outside the group. Their social position means they are likely to notice different things, identify different errors, and feel differently about what they see.

Similarly, class shapes interpretation: a media product that represents working-class communities from an apparent position of middle-class condescension will be read very differently by people from those communities than by those viewing them from outside. Age, nationality, sexuality and individual experience all contribute to the decoding position. This is why audience research that treats “the audience” as a homogeneous group is likely to miss the diversity of real responses to any media product.

A polysemic text is one that is open to several readings rather than driving audiences towards a single preferred interpretation. Polysemy is not a failure of communication — many successful and celebrated media products are deliberately polysemic, inviting audiences to bring their own meanings to the text. Hall’s model depends on polysemy being possible: if all texts had only one possible meaning, there would be no room for negotiated or oppositional readings.

Hall’s model contributed to a broader shift in media studies towards the concept of the active audience: the recognition that audiences are not passive recipients who absorb meanings directly, but active participants who construct meaning in the process of reception. An active audience brings cultural knowledge, personal history, critical thinking and social identity to every media encounter. This does not mean audiences can read anything into any text — the preferred meaning sets limits — but it does mean that the producer’s preferred reading is never the only meaning available.

lesson_title: Ownership: Conglomerates, Mergers and Integration
content_html:
What Is a Media Conglomerate?

When you watch a blockbuster film, stream a television series and read a news website owned by the same parent company, you are experiencing the reach of a conglomerate. In the media industry, a small number of very large organisations control a huge range of products across television, film, music, publishing, gaming, streaming and beyond. Understanding how they grow — and what that means for the content we consume — is central to the Media Industries framework.

A media conglomerate typically began as a business in one sector before expanding through purchases and deals. Over time, it acquires interests in television, film studios, music labels, newspapers, digital platforms and merchandise. The result is an organisation with enormous reach and significant influence over what audiences see, hear and read.

Key Fact

Media conglomerates grow through mergers, takeovers and demergers. A merger is when two companies combine; a takeover is when one company buys another; a demerger is when a conglomerate splits off parts of itself. All three reshape the ownership landscape.

Vertical Integration: Owning the Supply Chain

Vertical integration means owning multiple stages of the same supply chain. Imagine a company that produces a film in its own studio, distributes it through its own logistics network and shows it in its own cinemas or streams it on its own platform. At every stage, money stays within the same parent organisation rather than being paid to an independent supplier.

For a film and television conglomerate, this might mean owning: a studio that creates the content (production), a distributor that gets it to retailers and broadcasters (distribution) and a streaming service or cinema chain where audiences watch it (exhibition). Vertical integration gives enormous commercial advantages — and significant power over which products reach audiences and on what terms.

Horizontal integration means acquiring competitors or similar businesses at the same level of the supply chain. Rather than owning the whole chain, the company expands its share of one particular stage — such as owning several film studios, multiple television channels or several newspaper titles. The aim is to reduce competition and build market dominance.

Students frequently confuse vertical and horizontal integration. The key distinction is direction: vertical runs up and down the supply chain (production to distribution to exhibition); horizontal runs sideways at the same level (studio plus rival studio plus another studio). An extended essay answer that swaps the two will lose marks on analysis regardless of how well the wider argument is constructed.

Diversification and Synergy

Beyond integration, conglomerates also pursue diversification. A media conglomerate might expand into theme parks, merchandise, toys, clothing, technology hardware or food products linked to its brands. The logic is to spread financial risk: if one division performs poorly in a given year, profits from another division can compensate.

Diversification creates opportunities for synergy — where different parts of the same organisation promote and boost one another. A new animated film, for instance, can be used to sell merchandise, launch a theme-park ride, release a video game tie-in, generate a streaming series and drive advertising revenue across the conglomerate’s television channels. Every part of the business benefits from a single creative property.

Key Fact

Vertical integration tightens control along one supply chain; diversification spreads the business across entirely different sectors. Both strategies reduce financial risk and increase commercial power, but in different directions.

Concentration of ownership refers to the process by which control of media organisations becomes held by fewer and fewer large companies. James Curran and Jean Seaton, in their study of UK media power, argued that concentrated ownership is not a neutral economic fact — it has political and cultural consequences. When a small number of proprietors control a large share of the media landscape, the range of voices, perspectives and narratives available to audiences may narrow.

Their work draws attention to the gap between the free-market argument (that competition produces diversity) and the reality (that market forces tend to reward the largest players and push smaller producers out). Curran and Seaton’s analysis remains a key theoretical resource whenever an exam question asks about the relationship between ownership patterns and media content. The strongest answers use their argument to move beyond listing who owns what, and instead interrogate what that ownership structure means for the range of voices in the public sphere.

The Independent Sector

Not all media production sits inside large conglomerates. The independent or “indie” sector consists of smaller production companies that create content without being owned by a major corporation. Independent producers are an important source of creative diversity — they often take risks on distinctive or challenging projects that a conglomerate’s commercial logic would rule out. However, indie companies frequently rely on conglomerate-owned distributors to get their work to audiences, which means they are not entirely free from the power structures Curran and Seaton describe.

lesson_title: Production Processes and Working Practices
content_html:
From Idea to Audience: The Three Phases

Every media product — a television drama series, a magazine feature, a music video, a radio documentary — passes through three broad phases before it reaches an audience. Understanding these phases, the people involved and the technologies used is essential for explaining why media products look, sound and feel the way they do. The spec frames this as the relationship between pre-production, production and post-production.

Pre-Production: Planning the Work

Pre-production is everything that must be decided before a camera rolls or a microphone is switched on. It includes commissioning (deciding which projects to fund and develop), writing and developing the script, casting performers, scouting locations, drawing up a production schedule and agreeing a budget. The stronger the pre-production planning, the fewer expensive problems arise during filming or recording.

In television, a key pre-production role is the showrunner — the person who holds creative responsibility for an entire series. In film, the equivalent executive oversight often comes from a producer or executive producer. These roles shape the product before a single shot is taken, which is why pre-production decisions have such a strong influence on the finished work.

Key Fact

Pre-production includes commissioning, scripting, casting, scheduling and budgeting. These decisions shape the product’s genre, tone, form and intended audience before production even begins. Budget limits in pre-production often determine the visual style of the finished product.

Production: Making It

Production is the phase in which the actual filming, recording or other creative work takes place. A television drama may shoot on location, in a studio or a mixture of both. A radio documentary requires field recording and studio interviews. A magazine requires photography shoots, writing and design. Each media form has its own production conventions, but in all cases the production phase turns the pre-production plan into raw material.

Production teams vary enormously in size depending on the budget and form. A large-scale television production might employ hundreds of crew members; a podcast series might be produced by a single person with a laptop and a microphone. The size of the team, the technology available and the working environment all shape what kinds of product are possible.

Post-production is where raw footage or recordings are shaped into the finished product. For film and television, post-production includes editing, colour grading, adding visual effects, mixing the soundtrack and creating titles and credits. For music, it includes mixing and mastering. For print media, it includes layout, typesetting and image retouching.

Post-production has been transformed by digital technology. Work that once required large specialist facilities can now be completed on a standard laptop. This has lowered the barrier to entry for independent and lower-budget productions — and it means that post-production decisions (such as colour grading choices or editing rhythm) are now a significant part of the creative identity of a product, not merely technical finishing.

Outsourcing, the Freelance Economy and the Gig Economy

Major media organisations do not employ every person who works on their products. Much media production relies on outsourcing — contracting specialist companies or individual freelancers to provide specific services. A broadcaster might commission an independent production company to make a documentary series; a magazine might hire freelance photographers and writers for specific features.

This has created a large freelance economy in media. Many crew members, journalists, designers and technicians work on short-term contracts, moving from project to project. This gives organisations flexibility but can create instability for individual workers. Critics of the model, particularly in relation to digital media platforms, describe these conditions as part of a broader “gig economy” — one in which workers bear the financial risk of fluctuating demand rather than receiving the security of permanent employment.

Key Fact

Outsourcing reduces costs and increases flexibility for media organisations. However, it shifts financial risk onto individual freelance workers, creating a workforce that lacks permanent employment security — a pattern that has intensified in the digital era.

The rise of subscription streaming services has created a distinct working practice sometimes called streaming-first commissioning. Rather than making a film or series for theatrical release or broadcast window, a streaming platform commissions content directly for its own service — and may release all episodes of a series on the same day rather than one per week. This changes the economics of production (budgets and marketing are shaped around subscriber retention, not broadcast ratings) and can also change narrative structure (binge-viewing audiences tolerate different pacing than weekly viewers).

Understanding how the platform a product is made for shapes its working practices and form is a key analytical skill. A radio documentary, a social media vertical video and a prestige streaming drama series are all made through the three-phase process, but the personnel, technologies, schedules and budgets involved — and therefore the finished products — look very different.

lesson_title: Convergence and the Cross-Platform Media Landscape
content_html:
What Is Convergence?

Twenty years ago, television was watched on a television set, music was purchased on physical media and the internet was accessed via a desktop computer. Today a single smartphone can do all of these things — and a single global platform might deliver all three simultaneously. This blurring of previously distinct technologies, industries and platforms is what media theorists call convergence.

Convergence operates at several levels. At the technological level, different devices can now perform the same functions — a television set, a tablet, a laptop and a phone can all stream the same film. At the industrial level, companies that once operated in a single sector (say, a telephone network) now operate across content, distribution and platform simultaneously. At the cultural level, audiences engage with content across multiple touchpoints — watching a series, discussing it on social media, playing a related video game and buying related merchandise, often from the same parent conglomerate.

Key Fact

The specification identifies three types of provider whose convergence has reshaped the media landscape: content providers (who make media products), network providers (who transmit them) and platform providers (who deliver them to audiences). Where these were once separate industries, they are now frequently integrated within a single organisation.

Henry Jenkins and Convergence Culture

The theorist Henry Jenkins offered one of the most influential frameworks for understanding convergence. Jenkins argued that convergence is not simply a technological shift — it is a cultural one. He described a world in which “old and new media collide” and in which audiences move actively across platforms rather than sitting passively in front of a single screen.

A key concept from Jenkins is transmedia storytelling — a practice in which a single narrative universe extends across films, television series, video games, comic books, social media and other platforms. Each platform adds something unique; the full story only becomes visible to an audience member who engages across multiple forms. This is now a standard industrial strategy for major media franchises, not merely a creative experiment.

Cross-media ownership describes the situation in which a single organisation controls media products across multiple forms simultaneously. This differs from simple horizontal integration (owning several of the same type of company) because cross-media ownership spans forms — the same owner might control a newspaper, a television channel, a streaming platform and a social media property.

At its most complete, cross-media ownership creates what analysts describe as a “vertical stack”: an organisation that creates content, owns the network that transmits it and controls the platform through which audiences access it. This gives the organisation extraordinary leverage — it can favour its own content, control the terms on which competitors access the platform and collect audience data at every stage of the relationship.

The Second Screen and Platform Integration

Convergence is not only an industrial phenomenon — it shapes how audiences actually behave.
