Research consistently shows that many viewers watch television while simultaneously using a smartphone or tablet to discuss, search or react to what they are watching. This is sometimes called second-screen viewing. Media organisations have responded to this behaviour by designing content and marketing campaigns that actively invite second-screen participation — using hashtags, live polls and social media tie-ins to extend the audience’s engagement beyond the primary screen.

Key Fact

Jenkins argued that convergence changes not only the technology through which audiences receive media but also the cultural practices through which they engage with it. Audiences become active participants, moving across platforms and generating their own responses — rather than passively receiving a fixed product on a single device.

Convergence has accelerated the globalisation of the media landscape. A subscription streaming service based in one country can reach subscribers in over 150 countries simultaneously, bypassing the national distribution infrastructure that once made global media expansion slow and expensive. This has created intense competition among major platform providers — sometimes described as the “streaming wars” — in which organisations compete for subscriber numbers, exclusive content and talent.

The consequences for smaller national media industries are significant. When global platforms dominate the market in a given country, they can overshadow local broadcasters and independent producers. They also shape what kinds of content are commissioned — content with broad international appeal is privileged over regionally specific stories that might have strong local relevance but limited global market value. This tension between convergence-driven globalisation and national or regional media identity is a recurring theme in the Media Industries framework.

lesson_title: Funding Models and Commercial Industries
content_html:
Why Funding Models Matter

Where a media organisation gets its money shapes almost everything about the content it produces: what subjects it covers, who it targets, how independent its journalism is and whether it can take creative risks. The Media Industries framework requires you to understand the main funding models operating in the UK media landscape — and to explain how each model creates different priorities and pressures for the organisations that use it.

Public Service Broadcasting

Public service broadcasting (PSB) is designed to serve the public interest rather than generate profit. In the UK, the BBC is funded by the television licence fee — a flat-rate charge paid by households that receive live television or use the BBC’s on-demand services. Because the BBC is not dependent on advertising revenue, it can invest in content that would be difficult to justify on purely commercial grounds: expensive investigative journalism, specialist arts programming, minority-interest content and regional news that reaches smaller audiences.

The BBC has a public service remit enshrined in its Royal Charter. Other UK broadcasters also carry PSB obligations despite being commercially funded: Channel 4 is commercially funded through advertising but operates under a PSB remit; Channel 5 is a commercial broadcaster with a lighter PSB obligation. The PSB framework creates a mixed ecology in which public-interest content is guaranteed to exist alongside commercial content — but it is always subject to political debate about the appropriate level of public funding.

Key Fact

The BBC is funded by the television licence fee and has a full PSB remit. Channel 4 is commercially funded through advertising but also operates under a PSB remit. Neither model is purely commercial — both carry obligations to serve audiences that go beyond what advertising revenue alone would incentivise.

Commercial Funding: Advertising, Sponsorship and Product Placement

Commercial media organisations fund their content primarily through selling audiences to advertisers. Advertising revenue depends on the size and demographic profile of the audience: a product aimed at young adults will pay premium rates to advertise on a platform or channel with a large young-adult audience. This creates a structural incentive for commercial media to maximise their audience numbers and to attract the demographics most valued by advertisers.

Beyond direct advertising, commercial media can earn revenue through sponsorship and product placement. Sponsorship means a company funds or associates itself with a specific programme or section of content. Product placement means a brand’s products appear within the content itself — a character drives a branded car, drinks a recognisable beverage or uses a named piece of technology. Product placement is regulated in the UK: it is permitted in some forms of television content but must be disclosed with an “P” logo at the start of the programme.

Subscription models have grown rapidly with the rise of streaming services and digital platforms. Rather than relying on advertising, subscription-funded organisations charge users a monthly or annual fee. This creates a different set of incentives: the goal is to retain subscribers rather than to attract maximum advertising revenue, which means creating content that users value highly enough to keep paying for.

Many digital media services use a freemium approach — offering a basic version of their service for free while charging for premium features, ad-free access or exclusive content. This model attempts to maximise total audience size while converting a proportion of free users to paying subscribers. The tension between keeping the free tier attractive and giving subscribers enough additional value is a constant challenge in freemium media businesses.

The Media as a Global Commercial Industry

Media organisations do not only operate within national markets. The global media industry involves significant cross-border trade in content, formats and distribution rights. A television format created in one country may be sold and adapted in dozens of others; a streaming service commissions content to reach subscriber bases across multiple continents. This internationalisation of media commerce is part of the broader process of globalisation within the media industries.

Not everyone views media globalisation as neutral or beneficial. Critics have argued that the dominance of globally operating media organisations — many of which are based in a small number of wealthy countries — can produce a form of cultural influence that privileges certain values, aesthetics and narratives over others. This idea is sometimes linked to the concept of cultural imperialism: the argument that media globalisation is not just economic but carries cultural weight, shaping what audiences worldwide see as normal, desirable or prestigious.

Key Fact

Cultural imperialism is the concern that the worldwide dominance of media from powerful nations shapes what audiences in other countries see as culturally normal, potentially displacing local stories, values and production. It is a critical perspective on globalisation, not simply a neutral description of market size.

Not all media funding fits neatly into public or commercial categories. Some media organisations are funded through the voluntary or not-for-profit sector — supported by charitable grants, membership subscriptions or reader donations rather than advertising or licence fees. Community radio stations, local community newspapers and some investigative journalism outlets operate on this basis. These organisations are often able to serve audiences and cover subjects that neither commercial pressures nor public-sector commissioning priorities would sustain — but they typically operate with limited resources and face ongoing funding challenges.

lesson_title: Regulation, Digital Disruption and the BBFC, OFCOM, IPSO, ASA and PEGI
content_html:
Why Regulate the Media?

Regulation is the system of rules, codes and oversight that governs what media organisations can and cannot do. Without some form of regulation, media producers could broadcast harmful content to children, publish unverified accusations as facts, mislead consumers through false advertising, or sell violent video games to young people without restriction. The question of how to regulate — through government-backed statutory bodies, through industry self-regulation, or through some combination — is one of the most contested debates in media policy.

The UK has a distinctive regulatory landscape: different media forms are overseen by different bodies with different powers and different degrees of independence from government. Understanding which body regulates which form, and what type of regulation each uses, is essential knowledge for the Media Industries framework.

Key Fact

The five UK regulatory bodies named in the specification are: OFCOM (broadcast, telecoms and on-demand), IPSO (press), BBFC (film and video classification), ASA (advertising) and PEGI (video games age ratings). Each has a different remit, a different legal status and a different relationship to government.

OFCOM: Statutory Broadcast Regulator

OFCOM is the Office of Communications. It is a statutory regulator — meaning its powers are granted by Parliament and it has the legal authority to investigate complaints, impose sanctions and potentially revoke broadcasting licences. OFCOM was created by the Communications Act 2003. It regulates television and radio broadcasters, including both the BBC (in some respects) and commercial broadcasters, as well as on-demand services and telecoms providers.

Because OFCOM is a statutory body, its decisions carry legal weight. It enforces standards relating to accuracy and impartiality in news, the watershed (the 9 pm boundary before which adult content should not be broadcast on free-to-air television), harmful content and advertising standards on broadcast media. Its statutory status makes it more powerful than self-regulatory bodies — but critics argue that a government-backed regulator always risks political influence over the media it oversees.

IPSO — the Independent Press Standards Organisation — is the main self-regulatory body for the UK press. It was established in 2014 following the Leveson Inquiry, which investigated phone hacking and other press misconduct, and replaced the discredited Press Complaints Commission. IPSO handles complaints about accuracy, intrusion and harassment, and publishes rulings when publications breach its code.

However, IPSO is a self-regulatory body — it is funded by the industry it oversees and its membership is voluntary. Several major titles, including The Guardian, the Financial Times and the Independent, are not members of IPSO and instead operate their own editorial complaints processes. This voluntary nature is a key point in the debate about whether press regulation is adequate: critics argue that a regulator whose membership is optional and whose funding comes from the industry cannot be genuinely independent.

BBFC: Film and Video Classification

The BBFC — the British Board of Film Classification — classifies films and video content with age ratings: U, PG, 12A, 12, 15 and 18. These ratings inform audiences (and parents) about the suitability of content. The BBFC is not a government body — it is industry-funded and its ratings are advisory for cinemas, though local councils retain the legal authority to override BBFC decisions for cinema screenings in their area. The BBFC also classifies video-on-demand content for some streaming platforms.

ASA and PEGI: Advertising and Games

The ASA — the Advertising Standards Authority — is the self-regulatory body for advertising across all media in the UK. It enforces the Committee of Advertising Practice (CAP) codes for non-broadcast advertising and the Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice (BCAP) code for broadcast advertising. The ASA investigates complaints about misleading, harmful or offensive advertisements and can require advertisers to change or withdraw campaigns. Like IPSO, it is a self-regulatory body funded by the advertising industry.

PEGI — Pan European Game Information — provides age rating labels for video games: 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18. In the UK, PEGI ratings became legally enforceable in 2012, meaning that selling a PEGI 12, 16 or 18 rated game to someone below the rating age is a criminal offence (PEGI 3 and 7 remain advisory). This makes PEGI more legally significant in the UK than the self-regulatory models used by IPSO and the ASA, despite the fact that the ratings system itself is operated by a European industry body rather than a statutory regulator.

Key Fact

OFCOM is a statutory regulator with powers granted by Parliament. IPSO and the ASA are self-regulatory bodies funded by their respective industries. The BBFC is industry-funded with advisory (not compulsory) ratings for cinemas. PEGI provides age ratings that have been legally enforceable in the UK since 2012.

The existing regulatory framework was largely designed for traditional broadcast and print media. The rise of digital platforms, social media and user-generated content has created significant challenges that the existing regulatory structure was not built to address. Social media platforms allow billions of users to publish content without it being pre-screened by any regulator. Anonymous online speech enables harassment and abuse that would be easier to address in a named-publication context. Deepfakes (convincingly manipulated video content) and disinformation campaigns can spread faster than regulators can respond.

This has prompted significant regulatory reform. The UK’s Online Safety Act 2023 places new legal duties on large digital platforms to protect users from illegal and harmful content, expanding regulatory reach into areas that previously fell outside OFCOM’s remit. The tension between protecting people from harm and preserving freedom of expression is central to the debate about digital regulation: critics worry that overly broad online regulation could amount to government-backed censorship, while supporters argue that leaving harmful content unregulated constitutes a failure of public duty.

The question of who bears responsibility for platform content — the platform, the user, the internet service provider, or a statutory body — remains contested. Internationally, different countries have adopted very different approaches, creating a fragmented regulatory landscape for platforms that operate globally but face different rules in each jurisdiction.

lesson_title: Active and Passive Audiences and Uses & Gratifications Theory
content_html:
Are Audiences Simply Switched Off?

For much of the twentieth century, scholars treated audiences as passive recipients of media messages — empty vessels waiting to be filled. Today most media researchers reject that picture. This lesson explores the debate between passive audience models and active audience models, and introduces one of the most influential active-audience frameworks: Uses and Gratifications theory.

The Hypodermic Needle Model

The earliest academic thinking about media effects imagined audiences as passive. The hypodermic needle model — also called the magic bullet theory — emerged in the 1920s and 1930s. It suggested that a media message was like a drug injected into the bloodstream: the audience absorbed it directly, and the effect was instant and uniform across everyone who received it. Wartime propaganda and the growth of mass broadcasting fed fears that audiences could be manipulated at scale.

Albert Bandura’s social learning theory gave the passive model an experimental foundation. In his 1961 Bobo doll study at Stanford University, children who watched an adult act aggressively towards an inflatable doll were more likely to imitate that aggression than children in a control group. Bandura argued that audiences learn behaviours by observing media models — they do not need direct reward or punishment to acquire new conduct. This became a cornerstone of the media effects debate.

Key Fact

Albert Bandura’s Bobo doll experiment (1961, Stanford University) showed that children imitated aggressive behaviour they had watched, supporting the idea that media can teach behaviour through observation — the basis of social learning theory.

Two-Step Flow and the Opinion Leader

In the 1940s Paul Lazarsfeld and colleagues studied how political messages reached voters and found that media messages did not travel directly from broadcaster to passive mass audience. Instead, they proposed the two-step flow model. A first group — opinion leaders — engaged directly with media content and formed views; a second, wider group was then influenced more by those personal conversations than by the original broadcast. This weakened the hypodermic model considerably: audiences were not uniform, and social relationships filtered messages.

Think about how news travels after a major political announcement. A broadcaster airs a report. Some viewers watch it and form an opinion. They then discuss it at work, at the school gate, or online. Their friends and family update their views based on that conversation more than on the original broadcast. In a social media era this process happens at extraordinary speed: influencers, commentators and trusted peers all serve as opinion leaders, filtering and reframing the original message before it reaches most people.

Uses and Gratifications Theory

The decisive shift to active-audience thinking came with Elihu Katz and Jay Blumler’s Uses and Gratifications theory (1973–74). Rather than asking what media do to audiences, they asked what audiences do with media. Their argument was that people come to media with goals — they use it to satisfy particular needs. Blumler and Katz identified four categories of need:

Key Fact

Blumler and Katz identified four audience needs: information (surveillance of the world), personal identity (reinforcing values and self-image), integration and social interaction (maintaining relationships), and entertainment (diversion and pleasure).

The Four Needs in Detail

Information — also called the surveillance function — is the need to understand what is happening in the world. People watch the news, read newspapers, or check social feeds to feel informed and aware. A student checking headlines before going into school is using media for information.

Personal identity is the need to find values, attitudes or lifestyle choices reflected and reinforced in media products. A teenager might follow a YouTuber whose outlook matches their own, or a reader might choose a newspaper whose political stance confirms their existing beliefs. Media use here is about self-definition.

Integration and social interaction is the need to maintain relationships and a sense of belonging. Watching a popular television series means you can join conversations about it; knowing the result of a sporting event gives you common ground with colleagues. Even the parasocial relationships people develop with media personalities — caring about what happens to a favourite presenter — serve this social function.

Entertainment is the diversion function — using media to escape from routine, reduce tension and enjoy pleasure. Watching comedy, playing a video game or listening to music primarily for fun all fulfil the entertainment need.

Uses and Gratifications theory is especially useful for explaining why different people respond to the same media product in different ways. A documentary about climate change might be watched primarily for information by one viewer, for personal identity reinforcement by another (it confirms their values), and for social interaction by a third (they want to discuss it with friends). The same product — different uses. This also explains why producers design media products with multiple appeal points: they are trying to satisfy several needs at once to maximise audience reach.

One limitation: the theory assumes audiences are always conscious of why they use media. In practice, people often switch on the television or scroll a social feed out of habit rather than deliberate need-satisfaction. Critics also argue it ignores the structural power of media industries to shape which choices are available in the first place.

Gerbner and the Effects Debate

The passive/active debate runs alongside ongoing research into media effects. George Gerbner’s cultivation theory (1976) proposed that heavy television viewers gradually come to see the world through the lens of what television shows them most frequently. In particular, heavy exposure to violence in drama and news can produce what Gerbner called Mean World Syndrome — the distorted belief that the world is more dangerous than statistics show. Cultivation theory suggests that even if audiences are not directly copying behaviour (Bandura), long-term immersion in a media environment subtly reshapes their worldview.

lesson_title: Targeting Audiences: Marketing, Trailers and Viral Campaigns
content_html:
Who Is the Product For?

Before a media organisation invests in production, it must decide who the product is intended to reach. A target audience is the specific group at whom a product is aimed. The target audience shapes every decision — the storylines chosen, the celebrities cast, the platforms used, the price charged. Without a clear target audience, marketing spending is wasted.

A target audience is often divided into a primary audience and a secondary audience. A magazine pitched at women aged 25–35 may also attract younger or older readers who share its interests — those are the secondary audience. Producers do not necessarily design for them, but they welcome them.

Mass and Niche Audiences

Media products can target either a mass audience or a niche audience. A mainstream national daily newspaper tries to reach the widest possible readership; a specialist cycling magazine is produced for a small group with a defined passion. The economics of the two are quite different: mass-audience products attract large advertising revenues; niche products often charge subscription premiums because they deliver advertisers a highly targeted, engaged readership that is harder to reach through mainstream channels.

Key Fact

Niche audiences are commercially valuable because they deliver advertisers a concentrated, highly engaged group. Advertisers often pay a premium for access to a defined niche rather than broadcasting to a mass audience where most members are not potential customers.

Assumptions Organisations Make About Audiences

Media producers rarely have direct contact with their audience. Instead they build an audience profile — a set of assumptions about who is likely to be watching, reading, listening or playing. These assumptions are built from research: surveys, focus groups, ratings data and increasingly from behavioural data collected online. Assumptions can also be shaped by stereotypes of certain demographic groups, which is one reason why audience profiles sometimes reinforce existing inequalities.

Genre conventions play a part here too. A horror film producer makes assumptions about who enjoys that genre based on prior audience data — and those assumptions then shape the marketing approach, the certificate sought from the classifier, and the platforms where the product is promoted.

The trailer is one of the oldest audience-targeting tools in media. A trailer condenses the appeal of a product into 60–180 seconds, targeting the assumed audience through music, cast, pace, and the moments selected. A teaser is shorter — often only 30 seconds — and deliberately withholds more information in order to build anticipation and conversation. A taster, more common in broadcasting, offers a brief clip or preview episode to give audiences a genuine sense of the content without fully revealing it.

Each type of promotional material makes choices about what to emphasise and what to conceal. A streaming-era teen drama might release a teaser that focuses on the emotional relationships between characters rather than the plot twist at the series’ end, because the target audience’s interest has been identified as character-driven. Those choices reflect assumptions about the audience.

Viral and Guerrilla Marketing

Viral marketing attempts to generate audience momentum without (or alongside) conventional paid advertising. The goal is for audiences to share, discuss and amplify the content themselves — making them unpaid distributors of the marketing message. An effective viral campaign exploits curiosity, humour, emotion or social identity to motivate sharing.

Guerrilla marketing uses surprise, spectacle or novelty to create shareable moments. A product might appear overnight on city hoardings without explanation, leaving audiences curious; an unusual public stunt or pop-up installation might generate news coverage and social media posts without any paid placement. The logic is that earned media — coverage and discussion that isn’t bought — carries more credibility than advertising because it appears organic.

Key Fact

Viral marketing relies on audiences sharing content voluntarily across digital platforms. Guerrilla marketing creates surprise encounters in unexpected physical or digital spaces to generate word-of-mouth and news coverage. Both aim to reach audiences without relying solely on paid advertising.

Social Media Activations and ARGs

Contemporary marketing campaigns extend across multiple platforms. Social media activations coordinate posts, countdowns, and interactive challenges across platforms to build anticipation and engage target audiences directly. An alternate reality game (ARG) goes further: clues are planted across websites, social platforms and physical spaces, inviting audiences to become investigators who unravel a story. ARGs work especially well for products targeting digitally engaged younger audiences who enjoy participatory, puzzle-based experiences.

Marketing professionals think in three categories. Paid media is advertising you buy: sponsored posts, television commercials, banner ads. Owned media is content you control directly: your official social media accounts, website, and branded YouTube channel. Earned media is coverage and discussion generated by others: a journalist writing about your campaign, a fan community speculating about your product, or viewers sharing your trailer. A modern marketing campaign tries to convert paid media investment into earned media reach, which carries credibility because it is not perceived as advertising.

lesson_title: Categorising and Measuring Audiences
content_html:
Why Categorise Audiences?

Media organisations cannot sell advertising space or justify production budgets simply by saying “lots of people watch this.” Advertisers want to know which people — their age, income, values and habits. This is why the media industry invests heavily in audience research and categorisation. Three main types of segmentation are used: demographic segmentation, psychographic segmentation, and geographic segmentation.

The NRS Social Grade System

The most widely used demographic tool in UK media is the NRS social grade system, developed by the National Readership Survey and also used by JICNARS. The six grades are:

  • A — higher managerial, administrative or professional occupations (e.g. senior managers, doctors, solicitors)
  • B — intermediate managerial, administrative or professional occupations (e.g. teachers, nurses, junior managers)
  • C1 — supervisory, clerical and junior managerial occupations (e.g. office supervisors, sales staff)
  • C2 — skilled manual workers (e.g. electricians, plumbers)
  • D — semi-skilled and unskilled manual workers
  • E — those at the lowest levels of subsistence, including long-term unemployed and state pension recipients

Grade A and B individuals are often grouped as “ABC1” to describe an affluent, educated demographic; C2DE describes a working-class, lower-income grouping. These labels appear constantly in media planning documents and advertising rate cards.

Key Fact

The NRS social grades run from A (higher managerial and professional) to E (those at the lowest subsistence level). Grade A is not simply “wealthy” — it is defined by occupation type, not income level alone. This is the UK’s standard demographic segmentation tool for media audiences.

Psychographic Segmentation

Demographic data tells you who audiences are; psychographic data tells you how they think and what they value. Several frameworks exist. Young and Rubicam’s 4Cs model divides consumers by motivation. In the UK, the Values, Attitudes and Lifestyles (VALS) framework and variations on it have been applied to audience planning. Psychographic profiling allows an advertiser to target not just who a person is, but why they might want a product — their aspirations, anxieties and identity markers.

A streaming service launching a new nature documentary, for example, might target a psychographic profile defined by curiosity, environmental concern and cultural aspiration rather than simply by age or income bracket. The content and marketing would then be calibrated to speak to those values.

Digital platforms have moved beyond traditional segmentation by collecting first-party data — detailed records of what individual users actually watch, click, pause and search for. This behavioural data is far more granular than any demographic or psychographic category. A streaming platform knows not just that a user is a 28-year-old urban professional, but that they always finish crime dramas on weekday evenings, abandon romantic comedies after 20 minutes, and start a new series every 12 days. Those behavioural signals drive recommendation algorithms and inform commissioning decisions.

BARB: Measuring Television Audiences

The most authoritative television audience measurement in the UK is conducted by BARB (the Broadcasters’ Audience Research Board). BARB recruits a panel of households across the UK whose viewing behaviour is monitored electronically via meters on television sets and devices. The panel is designed to be statistically representative of the UK population. Data is collected daily and reported the following day as overnight ratings, with consolidated figures (including catch-up viewing) reported later.

The figures BARB produces — reach and share — are the currency of television commissioning and advertising sales. A drama that achieves a high overnight rating justifies its production cost; a low share on a Friday night might indicate poor scheduling rather than poor content.

Key Fact

BARB (Broadcasters’ Audience Research Board) measures UK television viewing using a representative household panel. It reports two key figures: reach (total viewers of a broadcast) and share (the percentage of the television audience watching a particular channel at a given time).

RAJAR, Pamco and Nielsen

RAJAR (Radio Joint Audience Research) performs the equivalent function for radio. Participants complete listening diaries over a set period recording what they listened to, when, and for how long. RAJAR data informs advertising rates and scheduling decisions across BBC and commercial radio.

Pamco (previously known as NRS) measures readership and reach for magazines and newspapers, while Nielsen provides global audience data including digital and streaming metrics. Together these bodies provide the quantitative evidence that underpins the entire commercial media economy.

BARB and RAJAR produce quantitative research — numbers and percentages that allow broadcasters to compare performance and set advertising rates. But numbers alone do not explain why audiences watch, what they enjoy, or how they feel. Qualitative research methods such as focus groups and in-depth interviews give richer insight. A film studio might commission quantitative research to discover how many 16–24-year-olds saw a trailer, and qualitative research to discover whether they found it exciting or confusing.

lesson_title: Reception, Active Audiences and Aberrant Readings
content_html:
The Same Product, Different Readings

Two viewers can watch the same television drama and come away with entirely different interpretations. One might accept the story’s values without question; another might find themselves resistant; a third might agree with some aspects and push back on others. Reception theory explores why this happens and how social variables shape what audiences take from a media product.

Preferred, Negotiated and Oppositional Readings

Stuart Hall’s encoding–decoding model (1973) established the framework for understanding the active audience’s role in creating meaning. Producers encode a preferred reading into a media product — the interpretation they want the audience to take away. But audiences do not always comply. Hall identified three reading positions:

  • Dominant (preferred) reading — the audience accepts the intended meaning. They share the values embedded by the producer and decode the message as intended.
  • Negotiated reading — the audience accepts the broad message but adapts or challenges specific elements in light of their own experience. This is where most real audience reception sits.
  • Oppositional reading — the audience understands the intended meaning but rejects it entirely, decoding it from a different value framework.
Key Fact

Stuart Hall’s encoding–decoding model (1973) identifies three audience reading positions: dominant/preferred (accept the intended meaning), negotiated (accept some, modify others), and oppositional (understand but wholly reject the preferred meaning). Hall’s model is in the Media Representations unit; revisited here for its relevance to active audience theory.

Aberrant Decoding

The concept of aberrant decoding was developed by the semiotician Umberto Eco (1965). Eco observed that when senders and receivers do not share the same cultural codes, the receiver can decode a message in a way that was entirely unintended — and this is in fact the norm rather than the exception in mass communication. A viewer from a different cultural background, historical period or social position may decode a media text in ways that diverge radically from any of Hall’s three positions.

It is important not to confuse aberrant decoding (Eco) with Hall’s oppositional reading (Hall). An oppositional reading implies the audience understands the preferred meaning and consciously rejects it. Aberrant decoding implies that the reader is simply operating from such a different set of cultural codes that the “correct” reading was never accessible to them in the first place.

The social and individual characteristics an audience member brings to a media text are called social variables. Age affects how audiences relate to cultural references: a viewer who lived through a particular event will read archival footage of it differently from someone who only encountered it in history lessons. Class influences what values and lifestyles an audience finds relatable or aspirational. Gender and ethnicity shape whose perspective an audience member feels positioned alongside or excluded from. Individual experience — personal history, occupation, beliefs — adds further layers.

A press photograph of a major public demonstration, for example, might be read as an inspiring act of civic participation by one viewer, as a threatening disorder by another, and as a media-distorted spectacle by a third — with each reading shaped by that viewer’s class background, political values and personal relationship to the issue being protested.

Key Fact

Social variables — including age, class, gender, ethnicity and individual experience — influence whether an audience adopts a dominant, negotiated or oppositional reading. The same media product can generate all three readings simultaneously within a diverse audience.

How Readings Change Over Time

A media product does not have a fixed meaning that stays constant across time. The cultural context in which a product is received changes — and so do the readings audiences generate. A situation comedy from the 1970s that was considered mainstream entertainment by its original audience might, when revisited today, produce widespread oppositional readings because social values around gender, race and class have shifted significantly.

This is what the spec calls changing cultural values. A viewer watching a historical product “re-reads” it through a contemporary lens. The reappraisal of past media is driven by shifting attitudes. It is also worth noting the reverse: a product seen as edgy or controversial at the time of release may later seem entirely uncontroversial as the cultural context moves on.

Active audiences often develop highly specialised ways of reading media products that diverge from any intended preferred meaning. A fan reading treats a text as a resource to be explored, extended and reinterpreted, often focusing on elements the producer considered minor. A queer reading looks for gender and sexuality subtext that may not have been intentionally encoded but is legible to an audience positioned outside heteronormative norms. A feminist reading foregrounds gender power relations within a text, often identifying ideological assumptions that were normalised at the time of production. All three are examples of active, positional reading practices that show audiences are anything but passive consumers of preferred meanings.

lesson_title: Media Practices, Identity and Fandom
content_html:
Media as Part of Daily Life

Media use is not something that happens in a separate compartment of life — it is woven into everyday routines. People check their phones before getting out of bed, listen to music while commuting, stream video during meals, and scroll social feeds late at night. These media practices are not random: they connect to who people are, who they want to be, and how they relate to others.

Media and Identity: Gauntlett’s Framework

David Gauntlett’s research — most fully developed in Media, Gender and Identity — argues that media use is a key resource through which people actively construct their identity. Rather than simply being told who they are by the media, audiences use media content to explore and develop a sense of self. Gauntlett distinguishes between the actual self and the desired self. Media products can serve both: a viewer might identify with characters who reflect their current identity, or they might be drawn to representations of the person they hope to become.

Gauntlett’s approach contrasts sharply with the passive-audience or hypodermic models. Where earlier effects researchers worried that audiences absorb media values without reflection, Gauntlett argued that the audience is always an active reader, picking and choosing what resonates. Identity construction is ongoing and selective, not a one-time injection.

Key Fact

David Gauntlett argues that audiences use media as a resource for identity construction, drawing on both their actual self (who they currently are) and their desired self (who they want to become). This makes media use an active, ongoing process of self-definition, not passive absorption.

Participatory Culture and Henry Jenkins

Henry Jenkins’ concept of participatory culture describes a media environment in which the boundary between producer and consumer has blurred. In Jenkins’ account, audiences — especially fans — are not content to passively consume media products. They discuss, critique, remix, reimagine and produce their own content in response. This was central to his 1992 book Textual Poachers, where he argued that fans actively “poach” texts, taking elements of existing media products and remaking them according to their own interests and desires.

Jenkins did not frame this as a modern digital phenomenon — fan creativity preceded the internet, through fanzines, fan letters and club meetings. But digital networks have dramatically accelerated the scale and visibility of participatory culture, making fan production (fan fiction, fan videos, commentary channels, cosplay documentation) accessible to millions.

Fandom describes both the state of being a devoted fan and the community that forms around shared devotion to a media product. Fan communities provide a sense of belonging, shared language and social identity. They mobilise around new releases, create rankings, theorise plot developments, and generate enormous amounts of secondary content. In the digital era, fan communities organise rapidly on social platforms, coordinating activities such as streaming events to boost chart positions or directing collective energy towards media organisations.

Contemporary “stan culture” — from the Eminem song “Stan” (2000), now used generically — refers to highly dedicated, sometimes intensely devoted fan behaviour. Stan culture shows both the creative and social power of participatory fandom and some of its less positive dynamics, including harassment of critics, extreme parasocial attachment, and fan communities turning on media creators when their decisions disappoint.

Key Fact

Henry Jenkins’ Textual Poachers (1992) argued that fans are active cultural participants who “poach” texts — taking existing media products and remaking or reimagining them according to their own interests. This is the foundation of participatory culture theory.

Parasocial Relationships and the Watercooler Effect

One of the most striking features of modern media use is the development of parasocial relationships. Audiences develop genuine feelings of familiarity, affection and even grief towards performers, influencers and fictional characters who will never know them. These relationships fulfil real social and psychological needs — particularly the integration and social interaction need identified in Blumler and Katz’s Uses and Gratifications theory.

Media use also generates the watercooler effect: a shared cultural text becomes a topic of conversation, connecting people who otherwise have little in common. A major sporting final, a dramatic episode of a serialised drama, or a divisive viral video all create shared cultural reference points that serve the social function of bringing people into connection with each other.

The Social and Cultural Significance of Media Practices

Media practices have significance beyond entertainment. The media contributes to shared cultural identity by providing common stories, shared news, and collective experiences. It fulfils individual needs for information, companionship and self-expression — particularly important for people who are isolated or who belong to communities not well represented in mainstream media. The ability to access online communities through social platforms and streaming has given niche audiences the opportunity to find each other and build shared culture around media products that mainstream broadcasters would never have commissioned.

Second-screen viewing typifies how media practices have changed in the digital era. Audiences no longer watch in silence: they are simultaneously tweeting reactions, looking up background information, reading other viewers’ responses, and participating in live comment threads. This transforms a traditionally passive act (watching television) into an active social practice. Media producers have responded by designing second-screen tie-ins, companion apps and live social activations around major broadcasts precisely because they know audiences are already doing this.
